prompt_topic: sacubitril/valsartan (angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition) in heart failure
raw_text:
Heart failure (HF) remains a major global clinical and economic burden, affecting millions of patients worldwide [1]. Over the past several decades, the therapeutic paradigm of HF has centered on suppressing neurohormonal overactivation, primarily targetting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and the sympathetic nervous system [2]. Although drugs like angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and beta-blockers have dramatically improved survival in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), patient prognosis has remained suboptimal. The discovery and therapeutic exploitation of the natriuretic peptide system introduced a key counter-regulatory pathway [3]. Sacubitril/valsartan is a first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) that acts as a single crystalline complex delivering both the neprilysin inhibitor prodrug sacubitril and the ARB valsartan [4]. Mechanistically, neprilysin inhibition prevents the breakdown of beneficial vasoactive peptides, including atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), and bradykinin, promoting vasodilation, natriuresis, and anti-fibrotic effects, while valsartan concurrently blocks the AT1 receptor to prevent the deleterious effects of angiotensin II [5].

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established sacubitril/valsartan as a cornerstone of HFrEF management [6]. This double-blind trial compared sacubitril/valsartan to enalapril in 8,442 patients with chronic HFrEF. The trial was stopped early due to overwhelming clinical benefit, showing a robust 20% reduction in the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization, alongside a 16% reduction in all-cause mortality [7]. Patients randomized to sacubitril/valsartan also experienced significant improvements in health-related quality of life [8] and a decreased rate of clinical worsening compared to the enalapril group [9]. Extensive post-hoc analyses verified that these clinical benefits were highly consistent across major prespecified subgroups, including age [10], glycemic status—additionally revealing improved glycemic control in patients with diabetes [11]—and baseline renal function [12].

To explore the safety and efficacy of initiating ARNI therapy during acute clinical decompensation, the PIONEER-HF trial was conducted in hospitalized HFrEF patients stabilized after an acute HF episode [13]. PIONEER-HF demonstrated that in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan led to a significantly greater reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels and a reduction in clinical events (such as rehospitalizations) compared to enalapril initiation [14]. The TRANSITION trial further supported these findings by showing that initiating sacubitril/valsartan in hospitalized patients, either before or shortly after discharge, was safe and well-tolerated [15]. Additionally, the TITRATION trial evaluated dose-escalation strategies, showing that both a condensed 3-week and a conservative 6-week uptitration regimen allowed a high proportion of patients to successfully reach the target dose [16].

The structural and hemodynamic impacts of sacubitril/valsartan have been thoroughly elucidated. The PROVE-HF trial showed that the rapid reduction of NT-proBNP following sacubitril/valsartan initiation was strongly associated with significant improvements in cardiac structure and function, including reverse remodeling and an increase in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) [17]. Simultaneously, the EVALUATE-HF trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan improved central hemodynamics, reducing aortic stiffness compared to enalapril [18]. In terms of renal protection, neprilysin inhibition maintains afferent arteriolar dilation and renal perfusion. Clinical trials, including UK HARP-III [19] and sub-analyses of PARADIGM-HF [20], confirmed that sacubitril/valsartan-treated patients experienced a slower rate of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) decline compared to those receiving traditional RAAS inhibitors.

Unlike HFrEF, therapeutic progress in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) has been incremental. The PARAGON-HF trial compared sacubitril/valsartan against valsartan alone in patients with an LVEF of 45% or greater [21]. Although the trial narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite endpoint of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death, prespecified subgroup analyses revealed substantial benefit in women [22] and in patients with an ejection fraction at the lower end of the study cohort (45–57%) [23]. To further explore these signals, a pooled analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF confirmed that the therapeutic efficacy of sacubitril/valsartan extends to mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) [24]. This clinical benefit was supported by the PARALLAX trial, which demonstrated substantial short-term biomarker reduction in HFpEF [25]. Furthermore, quality of life was better preserved in PARAGON-HF patients treated with the ARNI [26].

Reflecting this strong clinical trial evidence, international guidelines have been updated. Both the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) [27] and the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/Heart Failure Society of America (ACC/AHA/HFSA) [28] recommend sacubitril/valsartan as a first-line Class I therapy for HFrEF. While generally safe, clinicians should monitor for symptomatic hypotension, which remains the most common adverse effect [29]. Initial theoretical concerns that neprilysin inhibition could impair amyloid-β clearance in the brain and increase the risk of cognitive impairment were refuted by the PERSPECTIVE trial, which found no difference in cognitive function or cerebral amyloid deposition over 3 years [30]. Real-world registry studies and cost-effectiveness analyses further support the early and widespread clinical use of sacubitril/valsartan in contemporary heart failure management.
